summary: This RFC proposes another subnet addressing scheme that in most cases needs no change to host software. The drawbacks are that the number of subnets per network is limited and all gateways need modification.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal lets a network divide into subnets while leaving most hosts unaware of the division. Gateways combine subnet addresses when routing from farther away.

questions: what is the subnetwork addressing scheme in rfc 932
subtitle: A subnet addressing proposal designed to avoid changes to host software.

tldr.problem: A subnet scheme that put subnet bits inside the host part of an address would require changing host software throughout an existing network.
tldr.mechanism: This proposal assigns reserved Class C addresses to subnets. A gateway directly attached to the network uses the full address; a distant gateway drops the third byte and routes using the first two.
tldr.outcome: Hosts usually need no changes, but the method limits a block to 256 subnets and requires all gateways to learn the conversion rule.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 932's status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. This RFC is a proposed subnet addressing scheme.

sections.title: The Host-Change Problem
sections.content:
Earlier subnet proposals used leading bits from the host part of an address to identify a subnet. RFC 932 notes that this approach requires changes to host implementations, including systems already in the field.

This RFC proposes an alternative intended to avoid host changes in most cases. Its costs are a limit on the number of subnets and the need to modify all gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal aims to add subnets without teaching every host a new address rule. It moves the special handling to gateways instead.

sections.title: Class C Addresses for Subnets
sections.content:
The scheme reserves the upper half of Class C address space, identified by its high-order bit, for subnet numbers. A network using the scheme receives a block of 256 addresses whose first two bytes match. The third byte distinguishes the subnets.

Hosts and gateways attached to the subnetted network treat these as ordinary Class C addresses. A distant gateway recognizes the reserved pattern, removes the third byte, and treats the remaining two bytes as a Class B-like route, informally called a Class B 1/2 address.
sections.plainLanguage: Nearby devices use the whole address, including the subnet identifier. A distant gateway can ignore that part and keep one route for the wider network.

sections.title: Limits and Gateway Changes
sections.content:
A network can identify up to 256 subnets in one assigned block. To exceed that number, it needs two blocks and must treat them as two separate networks, although gateways between them can use a joint routing algorithm.

The main drawback is deployment: all gateways must understand the address-collapsing rule. A host that stores routing information for every Internet address may also need to understand it, though the RFC says this should not normally be necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The design avoids host changes but limits the size of one subnet group. Every gateway still needs coordinated software changes to apply the rule.
